scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Unlike most Tongan dances, the Kailao is performed in total silence except for a percussive beat, as speaking was historically viewed as a sign of weakness in battle.
This is Kailao. 19th century to present.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (Vwrq3xSbhAQ)
Title card: Kailao · Tonga · 19th century to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Kailao originated on the island collectivity of Wallis and Futuna (specifically 'Uvea).
It was introduced to Tonga in the 19th century and rapidly adopted into Tongan ceremonial life.

Historically, Tongan warfare did not include pre-battle challenges, as talking was considered a sign of weakness; however, the imported 'Uvean style provided a structured way to display martial skill.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance is used to display the dancers' discipline and skill with weapons.
It serves as a cultural challenge and a display of national pride.
The Sipi Tau variant is specifically used as a pre-game challenge to warn opponents and evoke Tongan identity.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Men perform the dance in a fierce manner that emulates fighting.
The lead dancer calls out the names of specific sequences and signals when to execute them.
Movements include mock combat between participants, rapid changes in formation, and technical tricks involving the pate kailao clubs.

Uniquely for Tonga, the traditional kailao is performed without singing.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers carry stylized clubs called pate kailao.
It is performed at both public and private ceremonies.
In a sporting context, such as rugby, it is performed on the field before the match begins.

scenes.title: The people
narration: King Tāufaʻāhau Tupou IV penned the Sipi Tau in 1994.
The 'Ikale Tahi (Tongan national rugby union team) are the most prominent modern practitioners.
A similar dance called the ka'loa exists in Rotuma, also derived from the 'Uvean original.
The dance is a direct import from 'Uvea (Wallis and Futuna) to Tonga.

music_brief.purpose: original soundtrack faithful to the tradition, with documented commercial reuse rights and no recurring royalties
music_brief.rights_rule: A composition brief does not clear an output. Record the provider/model/version, terms and date, input rights, output licence, restrictions and review before release.
music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Kailao (Tonga). New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.

wardrobe.policy: neutral dress with a respectful nod (palette and fabric only): the sources describe sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire, or the dance is sacred
wardrobe.from_sources: Dancers carry stylized clubs called pate kailao. It is performed at both public and private ceremonies. In a sporting context, such as rugby, it is performed on the field before the match begins.
care: every element traceable to the costume notes or a licensed image; nothing added for effect
no caricature, no exaggeration, no mixing of regions or eras
a culture bearer reviews the wardrobe before production; the review is recorded in the pack
